text: Section 206 filing rights are broadly available to different stakeholder groups, giving them the right to challenge existing RTO/ISO governance document provisions and give FERC the authority to investigate and modify these rates if they are found to be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, or preferential (“Federal Power Act” 2018). However, FERC is not required to respond to Section 206 filings. Compared to Section 205 rights, Section 206 requires a higher burden of proof for the filer. Under these rights, the existing rules must be found to be unjust, unreasonable, or unduly discriminatory, and the new proposal must be found to be just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. Exercising Federal Power Act Section 205 Filing Rights FPA section 205 gives the holder of the filing rights the ability to propose changes to certain governing documents (“Federal Power Act” 2018). When filing for changes, the filer must prove their proposed revisions are just and reasonable. FERC has a passive and reactive role to 205 filings, meaning it can approve, reject, make minor modifications, or make modifications with 12 The primary governing document is the RTO/ISO’s OATT, but may also include Transmission Control Agreement, Transmission Owners Agreement, Operating Agreement, and so on. 25 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. utility agreement to the proposed change but cannot propose an entirely new strategy or approach (U.S. Court of Appeals for D.C., October 1984). Beyond changing RTO/ISO governing documents, Section 205 filing rights are also important because they are the primary method through which transmission-owning utilities change their transmission tariffs. Section 205 rights can be assigned or shared differently in each RTO/ISO region; however, transmission-owning utilities generally maintain 205 rights over their revenues requirement and rates, and the RTO/ISOs generally maintain 205 rights over their open access transmission tariffs (OATTs) (U.S. Court of Appeals for D.C., July 2002).13 In many areas transmission owners must jointly agree on 205 filings related to cost allocation methods for regionally planned transmission facilities. There are also provisions in some RTO/ISO areas that allow state entities to add their alternative cost allocation method proposals to the 205 filing of the TOs or RTO/ISOs. Accelerating transmission investment depends, in part, on reaching successful cost allocation agreements to pay for new infrastructure. By examining legal disputes, current practices for allocating costs, and examples from different regions, this report highlights several trends and lessons that can support successful cost- allocation agreements. The legal cases show that cost allocation works best when it balances precision with practicality. It’s important to identify who benefits from a project and ensure they contribute to project costs.
